In this exercise, we'll practice setting up a supervised learning problem. Completing this exercise will help you be able to:

- Set up a supervised learning task: identifying the target variable and features
- Split data into training and test sets
- Train a model and evaluate its performance


# Getting Started

Make a Quarto notebook for this exercise. Here are the imports you'll need.

```{python}
#| echo: fenced
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, mean_absolute_percentage_error
import pandas as pd

import plotly.express as px
import plotly.io as pio
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"
```

# Wrangle Data

```{python}
data = pd.read_csv("../../static/data/ames/ames_home_sales.csv")
```

```{python}
data.info()
```

```{python}
data['sale_price'] = data.eval("Sale_Price / 1000")
ames = data.query('Gr_Liv_Area < 4000 and Sale_Condition == "Normal"')
```


# Set up the supervised learning task

What's the target variable? What are the features? What metrics will we use to evaluate the model? How will we evaluate the model on unseen data?

```{python}
feature_columns = ['Gr_Liv_Area', 'Year_Built']
target_column = 'sale_price'
```

```{python}
ames_train, ames_test = train_test_split(ames, random_state=42, test_size=0.2)
print(f"Training set size: {len(ames_train)} homes")
print(f"Test set size: {len(ames_test)} homes")
```

```{python}
def evaluate(y_true, y_pred):
    return pd.Series({
        'MAE': mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred),
        'MAPE': mean_absolute_percentage_error(y_true, y_pred),
        # 'MSE': mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred),
    })
```

# EDA

To keep this short, let's make only the most essential EDA plots.

```{python}
px.histogram(ames_train, x='sale_price', nbins=50)
```

Plot a scatter plot of `sale_price` vs. `Gr_Liv_Area` and color the points by `Year_Built`. I used a `marker_size` of 3 to make the points smaller.

```{python}
px.scatter(ames_train, x='Gr_Liv_Area', y='sale_price', color='Year_Built',
labels={'Gr_Liv_Area': 'Above Ground Living Area (sq ft)', 'sale_price': 'Sale Price (thousands of dollars)', 'Year_Built': 'Year Built'}).update_traces(marker_size=3)
```

## Linear Regression

```{python}
lr = LinearRegression().fit(
    X=ames_train[feature_columns],
    y=ames_train[target_column]
)
ames_train['linreg_prediction'] = lr.predict(ames_train[feature_columns])
evaluate(ames_train[target_column], ames_train['linreg_prediction'])
```

```{python}
ames_test['linreg_prediction'] = lr.predict(ames_test[feature_columns])
evaluate(ames_test[target_column], ames_test['linreg_prediction'])
```

Write a description of the model's performance on the test set in plain English. Include both the MAE and MAPE metrics. (Look at the [manual page for mean_absolute_percentage_error](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.mean_absolute_percentage_error.html) to see how to interpret the MAPE metric.)

## Decision Tree

```{python}
dt = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3).fit(
    X=ames_train[feature_columns],
    y=ames_train[target_column]
)
ames_train['dt_prediction'] = dt.predict(ames_train[feature_columns])
evaluate(ames_train[target_column], ames_train['dt_prediction'])
```

```{python}
ames_test['dt_prediction'] = dt.predict(ames_test[feature_columns])
evaluate(ames_test[target_column], ames_test['dt_prediction'])
```

## Compare the two models

```{python}
ames_test_by_model = ames_test.melt(
    id_vars=['sale_price'] + feature_columns,
    value_vars=['linreg_prediction', 'dt_prediction'],
    var_name='model',
    value_name='prediction')
ames_test_by_model['model'] = ames_test_by_model['model'].replace({
    'linreg_prediction': 'Linear Regression',
    'dt_prediction': 'Decision Tree'
})
ames_test_by_model['resid'] = ames_test_by_model['sale_price'] - ames_test_by_model['prediction']
ames_test_by_model.head()
```

Make an actual-vs-predicted scatter plot for each model. Use `facet_col` to put the two plots side-by-side.

```{python}
(
    px.scatter(ames_test_by_model, x='sale_price', y='prediction', facet_col='model')
    .update_traces(marker_size=3)
)
```

```{python}
px.box(ames_test_by_model, x='resid', y='model')
```


Write a brief description of which model worked better for this task.
